parties:
Joyanta Kumar Datta & others ------ Petitioners. 
vs 
Dilip Ranjan Datta and ors ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
4. The trial Court framed necessary issue and on consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the plaintiffs are not permitted to raise the plea that Joy Chandra Datta did not execute any will in favour of his wife Sura Bala and Sura Bala did not adopt defendant No. 1, as such, claim became barred by limitation. The trial Court accepted the defence case that Sura Bala Datta adopted the defendant No. 1 and ultimately found that the deed of will Exhibit-Ja and registered deed of adoption Exhibit Jha are genuine documents and the plaintiffs could not prove that the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 6 and 7 had any interest in the property left by Joy Chandra Datta and that their father Sudhir Chandra Datta alias Madhab Chandra Datta had no title in the property of Joy Chandra Datta. The trial Court also took the view that the plaintiffs could not prove their case as made out in the plaint. Accordingly, by judgment and decree dated 29-3-1994 the trial Court dismissed the suit. 

 10. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate and perused the impugned judgments and all other evidence on record. It is admitted that one Maya Ram Datta was the original owner of the suit land and he died leaving behind two sons in Ram Mohan Datta and Jugal Kishore Datta. Both the parties admitted that Joy Chandra Datta was a son of Jugol Kishore Datta who was one of the two sons of Maya Ram Datta. It is also not disputed that Joy Chandra Datta had a wife named Sura Bala. Since the original ownership Of Maya Ram Datta is admitted and his two sons Rain Mohan Datta and Jugal Kishore Datta are admitted, it may be inferred that the plaintiffs, who are the successive heirs of Ram Mohan Datta, could claim a share in the property left by Maya Rain Datta. The plaintiffs are not legal heirs of Joy Chandra Datta. They can claim the property of Joy Chandra Datta only as reversionary heirs of Jugal Kishore Datta, father of Joy Chandra Datta. The plaintiffs were conscious about the two documents namely, a registered will and a registered deed of adoption and before the written statement was filed claimed in the plaint that Joy Chandra Datta never executed any such will nor his widow Sura Bala Datta adopted defendant No. 1 as a son to her husband, Joy Chandra Datta. If the plaintiffs can avoid the will and the deed of adoption they may become reversionary heirs to claim partition of the property of Joy Chandra Datta also. After the death of her husband, a widow may adopt only if the husband of the widow and not to herself and adoption made by a widow to herself is invalid and it confers no legal right upon the person adopted under the Hindu law. The authority to adopt may be given to the widow only and not to any other person, even not to the widow conjointly with another as provided under section 454 of the Hindu Law. It is on record that Joy Chandra executed the will on 1-5-1922 authorising his wife Sura Bala, who was then pregnant, to take adoption twice. It is also on record that Joy Chandra could not arrange registration of the will as his health condition deteriorated and he was required to be taken to Mymensingh for treatment and he ultimately died. It is also on evidence that the witnesses to the will including the widow Sura Bala presented the will for registration and the will was ultimately registered on 23-6-1992. Section 32(7) of the Evidence Act recites that the wills are relevant facts relating to the transaction made by the will. The will has not been probated and for our purpose it does not require that the probate of the will should be obtained. The will is only relevant for the purpose of showing that Joy Chandra Datta authorised his wife Sura Bala to take adoption. Title to the property under the will shall not pass unless the will is probated and the decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the opposite party being 1993 BLD (AD) 160 provides (i) The executor or administrator, as the case may be, of a deceased person is his legal representative for all purposes and all the property of the deceased persons vests in him as such; (ii) In every case where either the will itself, or anything done under it by the executor, is challenged, proof of execution and capacity on the part of the testator, and of the appointment of the executor, would be required. The object of the section is only to get rid of this multiplication of proofs, probate once granted authenticates the will against all the world; it affords a ready means of proof of the contents of the will and it is a complete answer by the executor to any challenge of his authority as such. In the present case, we are not faced with any such situation. In the present suit for simple partition it is not required for this court to examine whether the will is a genuine document as the will or anything done under it by the executor has not been challenged excepting an averment that the will is antedated, fraudulent and fabricated. The plaintiff asserted that the will executed by Joy Chandra Datta was fraudulent, forged and antedated and the contesting defendants alleged that the will was duly executed by Joy Chandra Datta and was duly registered by the executor and witnesses of the will. The widow Surabala has been authorized by the said will to take adoption and, according to the contesting defendant, adoption was taken by performing the required ceremonies. Section 488 of the Hindu Law provides certain ceremonies relating to adoption which are (1) of the physical act of giving and receiving, with intent to transfer the boy from one family into another, (11) the Datta homam, that is, oblations of clarified butter to fire and (III) other minor ceremonies, such as putresti jag (sacrifice for male issue). The physical act of giving and receiving is essential to the validity of an adoption. Section 554 of the Hindu Law provides that the period of limitation for a suit to obtain declaration that the alleged adoption is invalid or never took place is 6 years from the date when the alleged adoption becomes known to the plaintiffs and this is also the limitation as provided under Article 118 of the Limitation Act. I am not required to go deep at this stage to investigate into as to whether the will and the deed of adoption were genuine documents as, in a simple suit for partition, such complicated investigation cannot be gone into. In 49 DLR (AD) 68 their Lordships of the Appellate Division held "In a suit for partition the court will, no doubt, consider the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land in some detail more than in a suit for permanent injunction, but it cannot in either case convert itself into a Court for determination of the respective titles of the parties if a serious dispute emerges from the pleadings as to the title of the plaintiffs to the parties' property and if it is not possible to effect partition without formally determining the plaintiffs' title to the property claimed in the partition suit. "It is not disputed that the plaintiffs claimed share in the property of Joy Chandra Datta as reversionary heirs in the facts of the case and found hereinbefore unless a decision is arrived at to the genuineness and otherwise of the will and the deed of adoption, it cannot be decided as to whether the plaintiffs are reversionary heirs to claim a share in the property left by Joy Chandra Datta. I am therefore, of the view that a complicated question of title is involved in that suit which cannot be settled in a simple suit for partition without claiming declaration of title. Further, right or wrong, a deed of adoption is on record which took place on the basis of a registered will and unless this deed of adoption could be set aside, the plaintiffs could not lay any claim on the properties of Joy Chandra Datta as reversionary heirs, inasmuch as the properties of Joy Chandra Datta devolved on his adopted son, the defendant No. 1, to the extent of full share as a natural son. In such facts unless these stumbling blocks are removed, the plaintiffs are not permitted to lay any claim on the properties left by Joy Chandra Datta. Admittedly, the plaintiffs claimed a share in a portion of the suit land as heirs of their father Sudhir but also claimed that they are reversionary heirs of Joy Chandra Datta. Thus, without getting rid of the stumbling blocks in the form of deed of will and the deed of adoption, no relation of the plaintiffs with Joy Chandra could be established to claim his properties as reversionary heirs. In such facts also I find that the suit for simple partition is not maintainable. The decision relied upon by the learned Advocate for the opposite party, namely, 1 Appellate Division Case 124 does not apply as the facts are distinguishable. In the said decision few letters written on different dates coupled with oral deposition of PW 1, the plaintiff and his two other witnesses found to be sufficient evidence that the suit land was purchased from the joint family fund. The facts referred to in the said reported case are also distinguished and have no application in the facts of the present case. In the decision reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 1471 it was held "section 213 of Succession Act creates a bar to the establishment of any right under will by an executor or a legatee unless probate or letters of administration of the will have been obtained." I have already noticed that the will is required to be probated to get title in the property but in the present case if the terms of the will are complied with, meaning thereby if adoption is taken by Sura Bala, the adopted son gets the property of his adopted deceased father by operation of law as a natural son and for such purpose probate of the will is not required to be obtained. Will is acceptable as a vital piece of evidence to prove that Joy Chandra expressly authorized his wife Sura Bala to adopt a son after his death.
